flashcards.f: What does the extensive form add relative to a static (normal form) game?
flashcards.b: It models sequential decisions, observation of past actions, and contingent plans. Timing of moves and the information available when a player chooses are represented explicitly.

flashcards.f: In a game tree, what are nodes, branches, the root, decision nodes, and terminal nodes?
flashcards.b: Nodes represent histories of actions; branches represent actions. The root is the unique initial node with no predecessor. Decision nodes are non-terminal; terminal nodes are endpoints where the game ends and payoffs are assigned.

flashcards.f: What three structural rules must a game tree satisfy?
flashcards.b: There is a unique initial node, and every other node is a successor of it (no cycles, no two roots). Each node except the root has a unique immediate predecessor. Each decision node is assigned to exactly one player.

flashcards.f: What is an information set?
flashcards.b: A set of decision nodes that a player cannot distinguish between. All nodes in an information set belong to the same player.

flashcards.f: What must be true of action labels within an information set?
flashcards.b: If the set has $k$ nodes, each action is represented by $k$ branches (one per node). Every node in the set must have the same number of branches and the same action labels.

flashcards.f: Give the lecture's formal definition of an extensive form game.
flashcards.b: A rooted tree with labelling functions: non-terminal nodes labelled by a player $i$ or chance $C$; chance probabilities summing to 1; information-set labels $i.s$; action labels on branches (identical within an information set); payoff vectors $(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$ at terminals; and perfect recall.

flashcards.f: What is perfect recall?
flashcards.b: Players remember their own past actions. They may or may not observe others' actions.

flashcards.f: When does an extensive form game have perfect information?
flashcards.b: When every information set contains exactly one node. Players then know the complete history when they move, and no other player's choice is still pending (no simultaneous moves).

flashcards.f: What is imperfect information?
flashcards.b: A player does not know which node in their information set they are at — typically because some other player's choice is unobserved, so moves are (partly) simultaneous.

flashcards.f: What is a (behavioural) strategy in the extensive form?
flashcards.b: A complete contingent plan $\sigma_i = \{\sigma_{i.s}\}_{s \in S_i}$, where $S_i$ is player $i$'s information sets and $\sigma_{i.s} \in \Delta A_{i.s}$ is a distribution over actions at information set $s$. It specifies behaviour at every information set, including those that may not be reached.

flashcards.f: What is a pure strategy, and how does it relate to a behavioural strategy?
flashcards.b: A pure strategy assigns probability 1 to one action at each information set. Behavioural strategies assign an independent probability at each information set. Under perfect recall, behavioural strategies are equivalent to ex-ante randomisation over pure strategies (Kuhn).

flashcards.f: In the lecture's perfect-information tree, why does Player 1 have eight pure strategies even though OUT ends the game immediately?
flashcards.b: Player 1 has three information sets (the root and two later nodes), each with two actions, so $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$ pure strategies. A strategy must still specify L or H at the later nodes after OUT, because a strategy is a complete contingent plan.

flashcards.f: How does connecting Player 1's two later nodes into one information set change the strategy count?
flashcards.b: Player 1 then has only two information sets, so four pure strategies: $(\text{OUT},L)$, $(\text{OUT},H)$, $(\text{IN},L)$, $(\text{IN},H)$. Player 2 still has $\{L,H\}$.

flashcards.f: How is the probability $P(z\mid\sigma)$ of a terminal node obtained, and what is expected utility?
flashcards.b: $P(z\mid\sigma)$ is the product of the behavioural probabilities along the path from the root to $z$. Expected utility is $U_i(\sigma) = \sum_{z \in Z} P(z\mid\sigma)\, u_i(z)$.

flashcards.f: What is the equilibrium path when play is pure?
flashcards.b: With pure strategies, only one terminal node is reached with positive probability. The equilibrium path is the path from the root to that terminal node.

flashcards.f: State the definition of Nash equilibrium in an extensive form game.
flashcards.b: A profile $\sigma^*$ is a Nash equilibrium if $U_i(\sigma_i^*,\sigma_{-i}^*) \geq U_i(\sigma_i,\sigma_{-i}^*)$ for all $\sigma_i$ and every player $i$. The definition is the same as in static games, but each strategy must specify choices at every information set, including those off the equilibrium path.

flashcards.f: In matching pennies with perfect information (Player 2 observes Player 1), why are there pure-strategy Nash equilibria?
flashcards.b: Player 2 has four pure strategies HH, HT, TH, TT. The plan TH mismatches at both nodes, so Player 1 earns 0 from either H or T. Both $(H,\text{TH})$ and $(T,\text{TH})$ are pure NE (and there are also mixed NE).

flashcards.f: In matching pennies with imperfect information, what is the unique NE, and does it matter who 'moves first'?
flashcards.b: Player 2 has a single information set, so only two strategies, H or T. The unique NE is both players randomising 50-50. The same normal form arises whether Player 1 or Player 2 is drawn as moving first, provided the first move is unobserved.

flashcards.f: The profile $(DB,Y)$ is a Nash equilibrium of the lecture's $D$/$U$ game. Why is Player 2's plan to play $Y$ not credible?
flashcards.b: If Player 1 opens $U$ and then plays $B$, Player 2's payoff is $0$ from $Y$ and $1$ from $X$. $Y$ is only (weakly) optimal while the subgame is unreached. Ex-ante Player 2 may plan $Y$; ex-interim they would switch to $X$.

flashcards.f: What is sequential rationality?
flashcards.b: A strategy is sequentially rational if, at each information set, it specifies a best response to the others' strategies for the remainder of the game, regardless of whether the player believes that information set will be reached. It requires ex-interim optimality at every information set.

flashcards.f: How does sequential rationality differ from Nash equilibrium?
flashcards.b: Nash equilibrium only requires optimality on the equilibrium path. Sequential rationality requires optimality at every information set, including those off the path.

flashcards.f: In the classroom Continue/Stop game, what does backward induction predict?
flashcards.b: At the last node Player 2 stops (90 rather than 0). Each preceding player then prefers to stop rather than continue into a stop by the opponent, so play unravels to Player 1 stopping at the first node for payoffs $(15,0)$.

flashcards.f: Describe the backward induction algorithm.
flashcards.b: Start at nodes that lead only to terminals; the player chooses the payoff-maximising action. Move one step toward the root, choosing optimally given how successors behave. Repeat until the root. In perfect-information games this always produces sequentially rational strategies.

flashcards.f: In the lecture's backward-induction example, what is the pure SPNE and the outcome?
flashcards.b: Player 2 chooses $a$ at 2.1 and $c$ at 2.2; Player 1 chooses $E$ at 1.2 and therefore $D$ at the root. The PSNE is $(DE, ac)$; the path is $(D,c,E)$ with payoffs $(3,3)$.

flashcards.f: Why can backward induction not be applied in the $D$/$U$ game?
flashcards.b: Player 2 has a nontrivial information set: the best response at 2.1 depends on whether Player 1 chose $A$ or $B$. The same game can even be drawn with Player 2 moving 'first' after $U$. Credibility must be imposed at the level of subgames, not node-by-node.

flashcards.f: What is a subgame?
flashcards.b: A subset of an extensive form that (1) begins at a single decision node, (2) contains all successors of that node, and (3) does not split any information set: if a set has several nodes, either all are in the subgame or none are.

flashcards.f: What is a proper subgame, and why may imperfect-information games have few of them?
flashcards.b: The entire game is always a subgame. A proper subgame is any strictly smaller one. If information sets span several branches, starting after an unobserved move would split a set, so there may be few or no proper subgames.

flashcards.f: What is a subgame perfect Nash equilibrium (SPNE)?
flashcards.b: A strategy profile whose restriction to every subgame is a Nash equilibrium of that subgame. Every SPNE is a Nash equilibrium (the whole game is a subgame). SPNE eliminates non-credible threats in proper subgames; in perfect-information games, backward induction yields SPNE.

flashcards.f: In the $D$/$U$ example, what is the unique NE of the subgame after $U$, and what is the SPNE of the whole game?
flashcards.b: After $U$ the simultaneous-move NE is $(A,X)$. Player 1 then prefers $U$ (payoff 3) to $D$ (payoff 2). The SPNE is $(UA, X)$ with payoffs $(3,4)$. Profiles such as $(DB,Y)$ and $(DA,Y)$ are NE but not SPNE.

flashcards.f: What restriction does Nash equilibrium place on off-path play, and how does SPNE repair it?
flashcards.b: NE requires sequential rationality on the path but places no restriction on off-path behaviour. If an off-path subgame is reached and play there is not optimal, players deviate further and the equilibrium unravels. SPNE requires Nash equilibrium in every subgame.

flashcards.f: When does SPNE fail to imply sequential rationality?
flashcards.b: With imperfect information, SPNE enforces sequential rationality only where proper subgames exist. If the only subgame is the whole game, a Nash equilibrium is automatically SPNE even if some off-path information set specifies a non-best response. Backward induction is not defined for imperfect-information games.

flashcards.f: What is a one-shot deviation, and what does the one-shot deviation principle say?
flashcards.b: A one-shot deviation $\sigma_i'$ agrees with $\sigma_i$ at every information set except one. In a finite game with perfect recall, $\sigma$ is an SPNE if and only if no player has a profitable one-shot deviation in any subgame.

flashcards.f: In the Stackelberg duopoly, what are the strategy spaces?
flashcards.b: Firm 1 chooses $q_1 \in [0,\infty)$. Firm 2 observes $q_1$ and chooses a function $q_2(q_1)$. Each $q_1$ starts a subgame in which Firm 2 is the only player; Firm 2 has infinitely many information sets, one per observed $q_1$.

flashcards.f: With $P(q)=50-q/2$ and $c=14$, what is Firm 2's Stackelberg best response?
flashcards.b: Given $q_1$, Firm 2 maximises $\bigl(50-(q_1+q_2)/2\bigr)q_2-14q_2$. The best response is $BR_2(q_1)=(72-q_1)/2=36-q_1/2$.

flashcards.f: What is the Stackelberg SPNE outcome in the lecture's example?
flashcards.b: $q_1^*=36$ and $q_2^*(q_1)=36-q_1/2$, so equilibrium quantities are $(36,18)$, $Q=54$, and $P=23$. Profits are $324$ for Firm 1 and $162$ for Firm 2.

flashcards.f: How does the Stackelberg SPNE compare with Cournot in the same market?
flashcards.b: Cournot is $q_1=q_2=24$ and profits $288$ each. Stackelberg has a first-mover advantage: Firm 1 produces more ($36$), earns more ($324$), and Firm 2 produces less ($18$) and earns less ($162$).

flashcards.f: Why does first-mover advantage in Stackelberg require commitment?
flashcards.b: Timing lets Firm 1 make an irreversible, observable choice. If Firm 1 could revise after seeing $q_2$, Firm 2 would anticipate that revision and sequential rationality would unravel Firm 1's leadership strategy.
